article.title: Apportionment as Geometry: Hamilton and Webster on the Simplex

introduction.p: In this activity you will treat apportionment methods as functions from a continuous quota space to discrete integer allocations. You will visualize Hamilton’s method and Webster’s method as geometric partitions of a simplex.
Throughout this worksheet we work on the simplex \Delta_4=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^3 : x+y+z=4\}.
Before working in triangles and three dimensions, we begin with the simplest possible case: two groups sharing a fixed number of seats.

Suppose two groups, A and B, are dividing 5 seats. If group A receives x seats, then group B receives 5-x. So every possible (possibly fractional) allocation corresponds to a point on the line segment 0 \le x \le 5.
In this warm-up, you will compare Hamilton’s method and Webster’s method in one dimension.

section.title: Quota Space on a Line
section.p: Think of x as the (possibly fractional) quota for group A. The quota for group B is automatically 5-x.

statement.p: Mark the integer points on the number line from 0 to 5.
What do these integer points represent in terms of seat allocations?

solution.p: The integer points are 0,1,2,3,4,5. The point k represents the allocation “A gets k seats and B gets 5-k seats,” i.e. (k,5-k).

statement.p: What does a point like x=2.7 represent in this setting?

solution.p: It represents a quota (ideal fractional allocation) where A “deserves” about 2.7 seats and B about 5-2.7=2.3 seats. An apportionment method will turn this into an integer allocation near (3,2) or (2,3).

section.title: Hamilton’s Method on the Line
section.p: Hamilton’s method works by first taking lower quotas and then assigning leftover seats based on the size of the fractional parts.

statement.p: Suppose group A has quota x.
(a) Write the lower quota for group A.
(b) Write the lower quota for group B.
(c) How many seats remain to be assigned after taking floors?

solution.p: (a) A’s lower quota is \lfloor x\rfloor. (b) B’s lower quota is \lfloor 5-x\rfloor.

(c) The remaining seats are 5-(\lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor 5-x\rfloor). For non-integer x, we have \lfloor x\rfloor+\lfloor 5-x\rfloor=4, so there is 1 leftover seat. (If x is an integer, there are 0 leftover seats.)

statement.p: Show that Hamilton gives the extra seat to group A exactly when
Simplify this inequality.

solution.p: Write the remainders: r_A=x-\lfloor x\rfloor and r_B=(5-x)-\lfloor 5-x\rfloor.
For non-integer x, \lceil x\rceil=\lfloor x\rfloor+1 and \lfloor 5-x\rfloor=5-\lceil x\rceil, so r_B=(5-x)-(5-\lceil x\rceil)=\lceil x\rceil-x=\lfloor x\rfloor+1-x.

Then r_A \ge r_B becomes
x-\lfloor x\rfloor \ge \lfloor x\rfloor+1-x \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 2x \ge 2\lfloor x\rfloor+1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x \ge \lfloor x\rfloor+\tfrac12.
So, within each unit interval [k,k+1), the “switch point” is k+\tfrac12.

statement.p: Find the value of x where the seat allocation switches.
Draw this point and label the intervals where Hamilton assigns:

solution.p: The switch between A getting 2 vs 3 seats occurs on the interval [2,3), at x=2.5.
For 2 \le x < 2.5, Hamilton gives A 2 seats (and B 3). For 2.5 \le x < 3, Hamilton gives A 3 seats (and B 2). (At exactly x=2.5 there is a tie in remainders.)

section.title: Webster’s Method on the Line
section.p: Webster’s method rounds to the nearest integer (after a scaling step in general). In the two-group warm-up, we focus on rounding behavior on the line.

statement.p: Suppose Webster uses the quota x directly. Write the condition under which group A is rounded to 3 seats.

solution.p: “Round to 3” means 2.5 \le x < 3.5. In particular, the switch from 2 to 3 occurs at x=2.5.

statement.p: Find the value of x where Webster switches from giving A 2 seats to giving A 3 seats. Mark this point on the same number line you used for Hamilton.

solution.p: The switching point is again x=2.5. Webster gives A 2 seats for 1.5 \le x < 2.5 and A 3 seats for 2.5 \le x < 3.5.

statement.p: Compare the Hamilton switching point and the Webster switching point.
Which one changes allocation earlier as x increases?

solution.p: In this two-group, five-seat setting, both switch at x=2.5. So neither changes earlier; they agree (except at exact ties).

statement.p: In your own words:

ul.li: How does Hamilton decide who gets the last seat?
How does Webster decide who gets the last seat?

solution.p: Hamilton: give everyone their floors, then give the last seat to whoever has the bigger leftover fractional part.
Webster: round to the nearest integer (in the full divisor method you first rescale by a common divisor, then round).

statement.p: How do these one-dimensional pictures help you understand what happens later in the triangle (three-group) case?

solution.p: They show how apportionment methods create “regions” separated by boundaries where a rounding decision changes. In three groups, the same idea happens on a triangle instead of a line: boundaries become line segments, and regions become polygons.

section.title: Barycentric Coordinates and the Simplex
section.p: The plane slice x+y+z=4 in the positive orthant is represented by an equilateral triangle. Each point corresponds to a triple with nonnegative coordinates summing to 4.

statement.p: Mark each point on the barycentric triangle and explain how you located it:

solution.p: One way: use that coordinates sum to 4 and grid lines parallel to a side keep one coordinate constant. For example, (2,1,1) lies on the line x=2 (parallel to the y-z edge) and also on the line y=1; their intersection inside the triangle is the point. Similarly for the others.

statement.p: How many integer triples satisfy x+y+z=4?
How many lie on the boundary? How many are strictly interior?

solution.p: Total integer solutions: \binom{4+3-1}{3-1}=\binom{6}{2}=15.

Interior means all coordinates positive. Count solutions to x+y+z=4 with x,y,z\ge1. Let x'=x-1, etc., so x'+y'+z'=1 with nonnegative integers: \binom{1+3-1}{2}=\binom{3}{2}=3. These are (2,1,1) and its permutations.
Boundary points: 15-3=12.

section.title: Hamilton’s Method as a Geometric Function
section.p: Hamilton’s method assigns seats by first taking lower quotas and then distributing the remaining seats to the largest fractional parts.

ol.li: Let r_i=q_i-\ell_i; let S(q) be indices of the s largest remainders.

statement.p: Suppose q=(x,y,z) satisfies
(a) Compute \ell.
(b) Compute the number of surplus seats s.

solution.p: (a) \ell=(1,0,1). (b) \ell_1+\ell_2+\ell_3=2, so s=4-2=2 surplus seats.

statement.p: Describe the shape of this region inside the simplex. Is it a triangle, a quadrilateral, or something else?

solution.p: Inside the plane x+y+z=4, the inequalities cut out a polygon (typically a quadrilateral) because you are intersecting a “box” in (x,y,z) with a plane.

statement.p: In the slab above (\ell=(1,0,1)), write formulas for:

solution.p: r_1=x-1, r_2=y, r_3=z-1. Using z=4-x-y on the plane, r_3=3-x-y.

statement.p: Suppose Hamilton assigns surplus seats to coordinates 1 and 2. Write the inequalities that express this in terms of remainders. Then rewrite using x,y,z and x+y+z=4.

solution.p: “Seats go to 1 and 2” means r_1\ge r_3 and r_2\ge r_3. In this slab: x-1 \ge z-1 and y \ge z-1.

Using z=4-x-y, these become
x-1 \ge 3-x-y \iff 2x+y \ge 4,
y \ge 3-x-y \iff x+2y \ge 3.
Slab: 1\le x<2, 0\le y<1, 1\le z<2 (with z=4-x-y).
Remainders: r_1=x-1, r_2=y, r_3=z-1. Need r_1\ge r_3, r_2\ge r_3, equivalently 2x+y\ge 4 and x+2y\ge 3.

statement.p: On the barycentric grid, draw the slab, draw the boundaries, and shade the region.

solution.p: The boundary lines are where equalities hold: 2x+y=4 and x+2y=3, intersected with the slab region. The desired region is the part of the slab satisfying both inequalities.

subsection.title: Step 4: Building the Full Hamilton Region

statement.p: For m=(2,1,1), list all possible surplus sets S.

solution.p: Here \sum m_i=4 and the corresponding floors satisfy \sum \ell_i=2, so there are s=2 surplus seats. Thus S must have size 2: \{1,2\}, \{1,3\}, \{2,3\}.

statement.p: Sketch all pieces corresponding to these surplus sets on the same barycentric triangle. What do you notice about how the pieces fit together?

solution.p: The pieces meet along tie boundaries where remainders are equal (e.g. r_i=r_j). The union is connected, and the overlaps (if any) occur only along boundaries (ties).

statement.p: Explain why Hamilton regions are intersections of floor slabs and halfspaces.

solution.p: Fixing the floor vector \ell forces \ell_i \le q_i < \ell_i+1 (a slab). Fixing who gets the surplus seats forces remainder comparisons like r_i\ge r_j, which become linear inequalities in (x,y,z) within that slab. So each piece is an intersection of a slab with halfspaces, and the full region for m is a union of such pieces.

statement.p: Describe what happens to the Hamilton output when a point crosses a remainder boundary. What changes? What stays the same?

solution.p: Crossing a remainder boundary changes which coordinate(s) are among the “largest remainders,” so the surplus set S(q) can change. Typically the floor vector \ell stays the same (unless you cross an integer boundary like x=1), so only the placement of the surplus seats changes.

section.title: Webster’s Method and Divisor Geometry
section.p: Webster’s method is a divisor method. Unlike Hamilton’s method, which works directly with the quota vector, Webster introduces a global scaling factor called the divisor.
Start with populations p=(p_1,p_2,p_3) and a seat total M=4. For a divisor d>0, define scaled quotas q_i=p_i/d, then round:

statement.p: (We will avoid exact half-integer ties.)

subsection.title: Step 1: Rounding Bands for One Coordinate

statement.p: Write the inequality that characterizes when \operatorname{W}(q_i)=2.
Express your answer as a double inequality.

solution.p: “Round to 2” means the number is within half a unit of 2: 1.5 \le q_i < 2.5.

statement.p: Interpret this inequality geometrically. What kind of region does it describe on the number line?

solution.p: It is an interval (a band) on the number line: all values between 1.5 and 2.5 are rounded to 2.

subsection.title: Step 2: Divisor Intervals for a Fixed Allocation

statement.p: For each coordinate, write the rounding condition in terms of d, then solve for d.

solution.p:
For coordinate 1 (target 2 seats):
1.5 \le \frac{p_1}{d} < 2.5 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{p_1}{2.5} < d \le \frac{p_1}{1.5}.

For coordinate 2 (target 1 seat):
0.5 \le \frac{p_2}{d} < 1.5 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{p_2}{1.5} < d \le \frac{p_2}{0.5}=2p_2.

For coordinate 3 (target 1 seat):
0.5 \le \frac{p_3}{d} < 1.5 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{p_3}{1.5} < d \le 2p_3.

statement.p: Explain why Webster can output m=(2,1,1) if and only if these divisor intervals overlap.

solution.p: Webster needs a single divisor d that makes all three rounded values correct at once. That happens exactly when d lies in the intersection of the three allowed intervals. If the intersection is empty, no single scaling works for all coordinates simultaneously.

statement.p: What does it mean geometrically if the three divisor intervals do not overlap?

solution.p: It means the three coordinates “want” incompatible scalings to land in their rounding bands, so there is no single rescaled quota vector q=p/d that rounds to the target allocation.

subsection.title: Step 3: From Divisor Intervals to Geometry on the Simplex
subsection.p: If we work in quota space directly, Webster’s rounding condition for output m becomes a set of slab inequalities: m_i-\tfrac12 \le q_i < m_i+\tfrac12.

statement.p: For m=(2,1,1), write the three slab inequalities for x, y, z.
Add x+y+z=4. Explain why Webster’s region is an intersection of three slabs with the simplex plane.

solution.p: Each slab restricts one coordinate to values that round to the desired integer. The simplex plane enforces the total seats constraint x+y+z=4. So the region is exactly the set of points on the plane that satisfy all three rounding constraints.

statement.p: On the barycentric grid:

ul.li: Draw the boundary lines x=2.5, y=1.5, z=1.5.
Shade the region where all three inequalities hold.

solution.p: The region is where x is between 1.5 and 2.5 while y and z are between 0.5 and 1.5, intersected with x+y+z=4. It is a polygonal region clipped by these boundary lines.

statement.p: Compare the geometry of Hamilton’s regions with Webster’s regions.

ul.li: Which introduces a global scaling parameter?

solution.p: Hamilton uses remainder comparisons (who has the biggest fractional parts). Webster uses fixed rounding thresholds (half-integers) after scaling. Webster introduces a global scaling parameter (the divisor), while Hamilton does not.

statement.p: Which method do you expect to be more stable under small changes in population data? Explain geometrically.

solution.p: Geometrically, both methods change only when you cross a boundary. Hamilton boundaries come from comparing remainders, so tiny changes can swap the ordering of fractional parts and flip who gets a surplus seat. Divisor methods like Webster tend to have boundaries governed by half-integer rounding thresholds after a common scaling, and are often viewed as more stable/regular in practice (though they still change on boundaries).

conclusion.p: In this activity you explored two apportionment methods as geometric functions. Hamilton’s method partitions the simplex using remainder comparisons, while Webster’s method partitions quota space using rounding thresholds controlled by a global scale.
